sections.heading: COPD (Emphysema)
sections.text: COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is a long-term lung disease that makes it hard to breathe. It includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Most COPD is caused by smoking. Quitting is the most important thing you can do, at any stage. COPD can't be cured, but treatment can ease symptoms, slow it down and help you stay active.

sections.heading: What is COPD?
sections.text: Your lungs are made of branching airways that end in millions of tiny air sacs. COPD damages them, so air can't flow in and out easily. It is usually a mix of two problems: Chronic bronchitis: the airways are swollen and narrowed. Many people have a cough that brings up mucus. Emphysema: the tiny air sacs are damaged, so air gets trapped in the lungs and you feel short of breath.

sections.heading: What causes COPD?
sections.text: Smoking causes most COPD: 80 to 90% of people with COPD smoked for a long time. Pipes, cigars and secondhand smoke also raise the risk. Symptoms usually show up after about 20 years of smoking. Dust and fumes breathed in over many years, for example at work. Other risks: a family history of COPD, low birth weight, and repeated lung infections.

sections.heading: Who has COPD?
sections.text: COPD is very common. About 16 million Americans have been diagnosed with it, and many more have it without knowing. It affects both men and women and is most often found in people who are middle-aged or older.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
sections.text: Shortness of breath, especially when you are active A cough that lasts for months, often with mucus Wheezing Chest tightness Frequent colds or chest infections COPD develops slowly, so many people don't notice symptoms for years, or think they are just getting older or out of shape. Sometimes symptoms suddenly get much worse. This is called a flare-up (or exacerbation), and it is often set off by a cold or chest infection. A flare-up can range from mild to life-threatening, so call your doctor if your breathing is worse than usual.

sections.heading: How serious is COPD?
sections.text: COPD is one of the leading causes of death in the United States. It usually gets worse over time, especially if you keep smoking. In later stages, people may be out of breath with very little activity and find everyday tasks hard. Treatment, and above all quitting smoking, can slow it down a lot.

sections.heading: How is COPD diagnosed?
sections.text: Your doctor asks about your symptoms and smoking history and examines you. Breathing tests (pulmonary function tests) measure how well your lungs work. This is the main test for COPD. A chest X-ray or other tests help confirm the diagnosis and rule out conditions with similar symptoms, such as asthma or heart failure.

sections.heading: How is COPD treated?
sections.text: Stop smoking. This is the best way to slow COPD down. Our clinic has a smoking cessation program to help. Inhaled medicines. Some are taken every day to prevent symptoms; others are used as needed for quick relief. Pulmonary rehabilitation. A program of exercise, breathing training, education and nutrition advice. It can reduce shortness of breath, improve your quality of life and cut down on flare-ups. Oxygen therapy if the oxygen level in your blood is low. Many people first need it only at night or during exercise. Surgery for some people with very advanced COPD, such as lung volume reduction or a lung transplant.

sections.heading: How can I stay as healthy as possible?
sections.text: Get a flu shot every year and a pneumonia vaccine, because colds and flu hit people with COPD harder. Stay active. Exercise builds strength and can make breathing easier. Ask your doctor before starting a new exercise program. Eat healthy foods regularly to give your body energy and help it fight infections. Avoid smoke, dust and strong fumes.

sections.heading: When to get help
sections.text: Call your doctor if you are more short of breath than usual, your mucus changes color or amount, or you have a fever. Call 911 if you can't catch your breath, or your lips or fingernails look blue or gray.

sections.heading: Asthma
sections.text: Asthma is a long-term condition that makes the airways in your lungs swell and narrow, so breathing gets harder. Symptoms come and go. Flare-ups are often called asthma attacks. There is no cure, but with the right plan most people keep asthma under control and live full, active lives. A severe attack is an emergency. Call 911 if your quick-relief inhaler isn't helping.

sections.heading: What is asthma?
sections.text: Your airways (bronchial tubes) carry air in and out of your lungs. With asthma, they are extra sensitive. When something bothers them, three things happen: The muscles around the airways tighten. The lining of the airways swells. Extra mucus builds up. Together, these make the airways narrower, so it is harder to move air in and out. Most attacks are short and get better with treatment. Sometimes an attack is so severe that it becomes life-threatening.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
sections.text: Coughing, especially at night or early in the morning Wheezing: a high-pitched whistling sound when you breathe out Shortness of breath Chest tightness, pain or pressure Not everyone has every symptom, and your symptoms can change from one attack to the next.

sections.heading: What causes asthma, and who gets it?
sections.text: Doctors don't know exactly why some people get asthma and others don't. These things raise the chances: Having a parent with asthma Having allergies Smoking, or breathing other people's smoke Air pollution, such as living in a busy city Fumes and dust at work, for example in farming, hairdressing, painting, and plastics or electronics manufacturing Lung infections in childhood Low birth weight Acid reflux (GERD) Asthma can start at any age, but it often begins in childhood. In children it is more common in boys; after puberty it is more common in women.

sections.heading: What sets off an attack?
sections.text: Things that set off asthma are called triggers. Common ones include pollen, dust, mold, pet hair and dander, smoke, colds and flu, cold air, exercise, strong smells, and stress. Your triggers may be different from someone else's, so it helps to notice what makes your symptoms worse.

sections.heading: How is asthma diagnosed?
sections.text: Asthma can look like other conditions, such as COPD, early heart failure or vocal cord problems. To find out what is going on, your doctor will: Ask about your symptoms and your health history Examine you Do breathing tests that measure how much air you can blow out and how fast. Often the test is repeated after you use an inhaler, to see whether your breathing improves.

sections.heading: How is asthma treated?
sections.text: The goal is to prevent attacks and keep you feeling well. Treatment usually includes: Avoiding your triggers as much as you can. This is one of the most helpful things you can do. Controller medicine , taken every day even when you feel fine. It calms the swelling in your airways so attacks happen less often. A quick-relief (rescue) inhaler , used during an attack. It opens the airways within minutes. A peak flow meter , a small handheld device you blow into at home. It shows how well air is moving and can warn you that an attack is coming, sometimes before you feel it. An asthma action plan , made with your doctor, that tells you what to take every day and what to do when symptoms get worse. For some people with moderate to severe asthma, newer medicines given as a shot (called biologics) can help. Our clinic offers allergy testing and biologic treatment for patients who qualify.

sections.heading: When to get help right away
sections.text: Call 911 or go to the emergency room if: Your quick-relief inhaler isn't helping You are too short of breath to talk or walk Your lips or fingernails look blue or gray A severe attack may need oxygen and medicine through an IV in the hospital.

sections.heading: Bronchoscopy
sections.text: A bronchoscopy lets the doctor look inside your airways with a thin, flexible tube that has a camera on the end. You'll get medicine to relax you and make you drowsy. Most people don't remember much of it. The test itself takes 15 to 20 minutes, and you go home the same day. Don't eat or drink after midnight before the test, and arrange for someone to drive you home.

sections.heading: What is a bronchoscopy?
sections.text: A bronchoscope is a flexible tube about as thick as a pen. The doctor passes it through your nose or mouth, down your windpipe and into the airways of your lungs (the bronchi). A camera on the tip lets the doctor see inside your lungs.

sections.heading: Why is it done?
sections.text: A bronchoscopy helps find the cause of lung problems, such as: Coughing up blood A spot or other change on a chest X-ray or CT scan Lung symptoms that can't be explained During the test the doctor can also take small samples to check for infection, inflammation or cancer.

sections.heading: Before the test
sections.text: Don't eat or drink anything after midnight the night before. An empty stomach keeps you safe if you cough or gag during the test. Tell us about your medicines , especially blood thinners. We'll tell you if you need to stop any before the test. Arrange a ride home. The medicine that relaxes you means you can't drive for the rest of the day.

sections.heading: What happens during the test?
sections.text: The doctor and nurse explain the test, including its benefits and risks, and ask you to sign a consent form. Your throat is numbed with a spray (lidocaine) so the tube doesn't bother you. A small IV line is placed in your arm. Medicine through the IV makes you relaxed and drowsy. You usually won't be fully asleep under general anesthesia. You get oxygen through a small tube in your nose. A clip on your finger checks your oxygen level, and a heart monitor (EKG) watches your heart. The doctor gently passes the scope into your lungs and looks around. The doctor may take samples to send to the lab. These don't hurt: Washing (lavage): a little salt water is rinsed into the airway through the scope and suctioned back out. Biopsy: tiny pieces of tissue, about the size of a pinhead, are taken with small tools passed through the scope.

sections.heading: After the test
sections.text: The whole visit takes about 1 to 2 hours, including getting ready and recovering. The test itself takes 15 to 20 minutes. Wait until the numbness in your throat wears off before you eat or drink. A sore throat, a hoarse voice, a mild cough or a little blood in your mucus for a day or so is normal. Someone else needs to drive you home. Call us if you get a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, or cough up more than a small amount of blood. Your doctor will go over the results with you once the lab reports are back.

sections.heading: Insomnia
sections.text: Insomnia means trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up too early, so you don't get enough restful sleep. Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of good sleep a night. Insomnia usually has a cause, such as stress, another health problem, a medicine, or sleep habits. Finding the cause is the first step. It is very treatable, often without sleeping pills.

sections.heading: What is insomnia?
sections.text: Insomnia is not getting enough sleep, or enough restful sleep, to feel and work your best. It can look like: Lying awake for a long time before you fall asleep Waking up often during the night and having trouble getting back to sleep Waking up too early in the morning

sections.heading: How does it affect you during the day?
sections.text: Symptoms are different for everyone, but may include: Trouble paying attention, concentrating or remembering things Doing poorly at work or school Moodiness or irritability Daytime sleepiness, low energy or low motivation Acting on impulse, or aggression Mistakes or accidents Worry or frustration about your sleep

sections.heading: What causes insomnia?
sections.text: Insomnia is usually linked to something else. Common causes include: Stress , from everyday work or family pressures to big changes like a death, divorce or job loss. Other sleep disorders. For example, people with restless legs syndrome often have trouble falling asleep, and sleep apnea can wake you many times a night. Medical conditions. Pain, discomfort or limited mobility can make sleep hard. This is more common in older adults. Pregnancy (especially the last three months) and menopause can also disturb sleep. Mental health. Depression and anxiety are common causes of trouble falling or staying asleep. Sometimes insomnia is the first sign of them. Bipolar disorder and other mood disorders can also affect sleep. Medicines and substances. Some cold and allergy medicines (containing pseudoephedrine), antidepressants, and medicines for ADHD, high blood pressure or Parkinson's disease can keep you awake. Caffeine and other stimulants make it hard to fall asleep. Alcohol before bed causes you to wake during the night. Stopping a sleeping pill suddenly can also cause insomnia. Your bedroom. Noise, light, a room that is too hot or cold, or a bed partner who snores can all disrupt sleep. Habits and schedules. Going to bed at different times, or working shifts and sleeping during the day, can throw off your body clock.

sections.heading: Simple habits that help
sections.text: Go to bed and get up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Keep your bedroom dark, quiet and cool, and use your bed only for sleep. Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening, and avoid alcohol close to bedtime. Put screens away for the last hour before bed and do something relaxing. If you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something quiet until you feel sleepy.

sections.heading: How is insomnia treated?
sections.text: We start by looking for the cause, such as another sleep disorder, a medical problem or a medicine. Treating that often improves sleep. Other treatments include: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I): a short program that changes the thoughts and habits that keep you awake. It is the recommended first treatment for long-term insomnia and works well for most people. Medicines for short-term use in some cases, chosen carefully with your doctor. A sleep study if your doctor suspects another sleep disorder, such as sleep apnea. If poor sleep has lasted more than a few weeks or is affecting your days, talk to us. Our clinic offers sleep evaluations and an insomnia handout on the Patient Forms page.

sections.heading: Lung Cancer
sections.text: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, for both men and women. Smoking causes about 85% of cases. Quitting at any age lowers your risk. Early lung cancer often has no symptoms. If you smoke or used to smoke, ask whether a yearly screening scan is right for you. Treatment depends on the type of lung cancer and how far it has spread.

sections.heading: What is lung cancer?
sections.text: Lung cancer starts when cells in the lung begin to grow out of control. Over time they form a lump, called a tumor. If it isn't treated, cancer can spread to other parts of the body, such as the lymph nodes, bones, liver, adrenal glands or brain. This spread is called metastasis. There are two main types, which grow and are treated differently.

sections.heading: Non-small cell lung cancer
sections.text: This is the most common type, about 85% of lung cancers. It usually grows more slowly than small cell lung cancer. The main kinds are: Adenocarcinoma , the most common lung cancer in the United States. It is linked to smoking, but it is also the most common type in people who have never smoked. Squamous cell carcinoma , about 25% of lung cancers. It usually starts in the larger airways and is most often caused by smoking. Large cell carcinoma , a less common type that doesn't fit the other two groups.

sections.heading: Small cell lung cancer
sections.text: This type makes up about 15% of lung cancers and is almost always caused by smoking. The cancer cells are small but divide quickly, so it tends to grow and spread fast. Doctors describe it as limited (only in the chest) or extensive (spread beyond the chest). It usually responds to chemotherapy but is hard to cure.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
sections.text: Lung cancer often causes no symptoms until it is advanced. When symptoms do appear, they may include: A cough that doesn't go away or gets worse Coughing up blood Shortness of breath Pain in the chest, shoulders or back Weight loss or loss of appetite Bronchitis or pneumonia that keeps coming back Swelling of the face or arms These symptoms often have other causes, but see a doctor if you have any of them, especially if you smoke or used to smoke.

sections.heading: What causes lung cancer?
sections.text: Smoking cigarettes, pipes or cigars causes about 85% of lung cancers. Tobacco smoke contains thousands of chemicals, many of which are known to cause cancer. Secondhand smoke from other people's tobacco. Radon , a natural gas with no smell or color that can seep into homes from the ground. A simple home test can check for it. Chemicals at work , such as asbestos, nickel and silica. Family history of lung cancer. Other lung diseases , such as COPD or pulmonary fibrosis. A diet low in fruits, vegetables and grains may also raise the risk.

sections.heading: How common is lung cancer?
sections.text: More than 200,000 Americans are diagnosed with lung cancer each year. About 1 in 16 people will get it during their lifetime. It is most common in people over 50 with a long history of smoking.

sections.heading: Screening: finding it early
sections.text: Finding lung cancer early, before it spreads, gives the best chance of successful treatment. A yearly low-dose CT scan of the chest is recommended for adults who: are 50 to 80 years old, and have smoked at least 20 "pack-years" (for example, a pack a day for 20 years, or two packs a day for 10 years), and still smoke or quit within the past 15 years. If this sounds like you, ask us whether screening is right for you.

sections.heading: How is lung cancer diagnosed?
sections.text: Your doctor may use one or more of these tests: Imaging: a chest X-ray, CT scan, PET scan or MRI to look for tumors and see whether cancer has spread. Sputum test: mucus you cough up is checked for cancer cells. Biopsy: a small piece of tissue is removed and checked under a microscope. This is the only way to know for sure. It can be done during a bronchoscopy , with a thin needle passed through the skin using a CT scan as a guide, or with a small surgical procedure. Once cancer is found, more tests show how far it has spread. This is called staging , and it helps your doctor plan treatment.

sections.heading: How is lung cancer treated?
sections.text: Surgery to remove the cancer is often the best option for early non-small cell lung cancer. Depending on the tumor, the surgeon may remove a small wedge of lung, a whole section (lobe), or rarely an entire lung. Radiation therapy uses high-energy rays to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. Chemotherapy uses medicines that travel through the body to kill cancer cells, including cells that have spread beyond the lungs. Targeted therapy and immunotherapy are newer medicines. Targeted drugs attack specific changes in the cancer cells; immunotherapy helps your immune system fight the cancer. Clinical trials test new treatments and are open to patients at every stage. Treatments are often combined. Even when cancer can't be cured, treatment can ease symptoms, improve quality of life and help people live longer.

sections.heading: What is the outlook?
sections.text: The outlook depends on the type of lung cancer, its stage, the size of the tumor, whether there are symptoms, and your overall health. Finding it early makes the biggest difference.

sections.heading: Can lung cancer be prevented?
sections.text: Don't smoke, or quit. It is never too late, and we can help. Avoid secondhand smoke. Test your home for radon. Take safety precautions if you work around asbestos or other chemicals. Eat plenty of fruits and vegetables.

sections.heading: Narcolepsy
sections.text: Narcolepsy is a long-term brain condition that causes strong sleepiness during the day, no matter how much sleep you get at night. People with narcolepsy can fall asleep suddenly, even while working, talking or driving. It is uncommon, affecting about 1 in 2,000 people, and often starts in the teen or young adult years. There is no cure, but treatment can control symptoms well.

sections.heading: What is narcolepsy?
sections.text: Normally the brain keeps sleep and wakefulness separate. In narcolepsy, the brain has trouble controlling when you are asleep and awake, so pieces of sleep spill into the day. People feel an overwhelming need to sleep and can drift off at any time. These "sleep attacks" can last from 30 seconds to more than 30 minutes. Narcolepsy can start at any age, but it most often begins in the teens or early adulthood. Because the sleepiness is often mistaken for laziness, depression or not getting enough sleep, many people go years before being diagnosed.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
sections.text: Excessive daytime sleepiness. This is the main symptom and happens to everyone with narcolepsy. Sudden loss of muscle control (cataplexy). Brief weakness, such as a sagging face, drooping head or buckling knees, often set off by strong emotions like laughing or surprise. You stay awake during it. Not everyone has this symptom. Sleep paralysis. Being unable to move or speak for a short time while falling asleep or waking up. It can be frightening, but it passes and is not harmful. Vivid, dream-like images when drifting off to sleep or waking up, which can feel very real. Broken night sleep , waking up many times during the night.

sections.heading: What causes it?
sections.text: In many people with narcolepsy, the brain has lost cells that make a chemical called hypocretin (also called orexin), which helps keep you awake. Researchers think the immune system may attack these cells by mistake. Genes may also play a part. For some people, the cause isn't known.

sections.heading: How is narcolepsy diagnosed?
sections.text: Your doctor asks about your sleep and your symptoms. You may be asked to keep a sleep diary for a week or two. An overnight sleep study checks your sleep and rules out other problems, such as sleep apnea. The next day, a Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) measures how quickly you fall asleep during a series of short daytime naps, and whether you go straight into dreaming sleep. Our sleep lab does both tests.

sections.heading: How is narcolepsy treated?
sections.text: Narcolepsy can't be cured, but most people manage it well with a mix of medicine and daily habits: Medicines to help you stay awake during the day, and others that reduce cataplexy and improve night sleep. Your doctor will find what works best for you. Short, planned naps during the day can boost alertness. A regular sleep schedule , going to bed and waking up at the same times every day. Avoiding alcohol and heavy meals before important activities, since they can make sleepiness worse.

sections.heading: Staying safe
sections.text: Don't drive or use dangerous machines if you feel sleepy. Talk with your doctor about when it is safe to drive. It can also help to tell your school or workplace, so they can allow for naps or schedule changes. If you are often very sleepy during the day even after a full night's sleep, talk to us. It may be narcolepsy or another sleep disorder that can be treated.

sections.heading: Parasomnia
sections.text: Parasomnias are unusual things people do or experience while falling asleep, sleeping or waking up, such as sleepwalking or night terrors. They are common in children, who often grow out of them, but adults can have them too. Most aren't dangerous, but some can lead to injuries, so safety matters. A sleep doctor can find the cause and help.

sections.heading: What are parasomnias?
sections.text: Parasomnias are a group of sleep disorders that involve unusual movements, behaviors, feelings or dreams. They can happen as you fall asleep, while you sleep, between stages of sleep, or as you wake up. The person usually doesn't remember them the next day.

sections.heading: Common types
sections.text: Night terrors. The person suddenly sits up screaming or crying and looks terrified, but is not really awake and is hard to comfort. Most common in children. Sleepwalking. Getting up and walking around, or doing other activities, while still asleep. Sleep talking. Talking during sleep, from a few words to long conversations. It is usually harmless. Sleep-related eating disorder (SRED). Eating while partly asleep, often large amounts or unusual foods, with little or no memory of it. REM behavior disorder (RBD). Normally your body is still while you dream. In RBD it isn't, so people "act out" their dreams by talking, shouting, punching or kicking, and can hurt themselves or a bed partner.

sections.heading: What causes them?
sections.text: Parasomnias often run in families. Things that can set them off or make them worse include: Not getting enough sleep, or an irregular sleep schedule Stress Alcohol and some medicines, including some sleeping pills Other sleep problems, such as sleep apnea or restless legs syndrome Fever or illness REM behavior disorder is most common in men over 50. It is sometimes linked to other conditions of the nervous system, so it is important to have it checked by a doctor.

sections.heading: Keeping safe at night
sections.text: Lock outside doors and windows, and consider door alarms or bells. Remove sharp or breakable objects and clutter near the bed. Put gates at the top of stairs if someone sleepwalks. For REM behavior disorder, pad the area around the bed or move the bed away from windows. A bed partner may need to sleep separately until it is treated. Gently guide a sleepwalker back to bed rather than trying to wake them.

sections.heading: How are they diagnosed and treated?
sections.text: Your doctor will ask about what happens during the night. A bed partner or family member's description, or a video taken at home, can help a lot. An overnight sleep study records your brain activity, breathing and movements while you sleep, and can also find other problems, such as sleep apnea, that may be setting off the episodes. Treatment depends on the type and cause. It may include getting more regular sleep, reducing stress, changing medicines, treating another sleep disorder, and in some cases medicine to calm the episodes. See a doctor if episodes are frequent, dangerous, disturb others in the home, or leave you sleepy during the day.

sections.heading: Pulmonologist
sections.text: A pulmonologist is a doctor who specializes in the lungs and breathing. Your regular doctor may send you to one for a cough that won't go away, shortness of breath, an abnormal chest X-ray or CT scan, or lung infections that keep coming back. Most visits start with a chest X-ray and simple breathing tests. Below is a short guide to the tests you might have.

sections.heading: What does a pulmonologist do?
sections.text: Pulmonology is a specialty of internal medicine. Pulmonologists diagnose and treat diseases of the lungs and airways, including: Lung infections, short-term and long-term Asthma, COPD and chronic bronchitis Lung cancer Blood clots in the lungs (pulmonary embolism) Fluid around the lungs (pleural effusion) High blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension) Scarring of the lungs (pulmonary fibrosis) Lung disease from work, such as asbestosis or silicosis

sections.heading: Chest X-ray
sections.text: A quick, painless picture of your chest. It can show or rule out many common problems, such as pneumonia, heart failure, fluid around the lungs and tumors. Your doctor will go over the results with you.

sections.heading: CT scan
sections.text: A CT scan uses X-rays and a computer to make detailed pictures that look like thin slices of your chest, a bit like slices of a loaf of bread. It shows the lungs, blood vessels and lymph nodes much more clearly than a regular X-ray. Some CT scans use contrast dye given through an IV. Before a scan with contrast, tell your doctor if you take the diabetes medicine metformin (Glucophage), have kidney disease, or are allergic to iodine or contrast dye.

sections.heading: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan
sections.text: An outpatient test done in the hospital's nuclear medicine department. It compares where air goes in your lungs with where blood flows. It is mostly used to check for a blood clot in the lungs: a clot shows up as an area that gets air but not enough blood.

sections.heading: Pulmonary function testing (breathing tests)
sections.text: You breathe in and out through a mouthpiece while a machine measures how much air your lungs hold and how fast you can move it. These tests help sort lung problems into types, such as asthma or COPD (where air has trouble getting out) or scarring of the lungs (where the lungs can't fully expand). They also measure how well oxygen passes from your lungs into your blood. Sometimes you repeat the test after using an inhaler to see whether your airways open up, which is a sign of asthma. A related test, the methacholine challenge , has you breathe in a medicine that can briefly narrow sensitive airways, to check for asthma when other tests are unclear.

sections.heading: Arterial blood gas
sections.text: A blood sample, usually taken from an artery in the wrist, shows how well your lungs bring in oxygen and get rid of carbon dioxide. It can also help check whether surgery is safe for people with lung disease.

sections.heading: 6-minute walk test
sections.text: You walk at your own pace for six minutes while we record the distance and check your breathing, heart rate and oxygen level. Repeating the test over time shows whether a lung condition is getting better or worse.

sections.heading: Ambulatory oximetry
sections.text: A small clip on your finger measures the oxygen in your blood while you rest and then while you walk. It shows whether your oxygen drops with activity and whether you need extra oxygen.

sections.heading: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing
sections.text: You exercise, usually on a stationary bike, while your heart and lungs are monitored. It helps find out whether shortness of breath is coming from your heart, your lungs, or something else.

sections.heading: Bronchoscopy
sections.text: A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through your nose or mouth into your lungs while you are sedated, so it is not usually uncomfortable. The doctor can look at your airways and take small samples, such as a rinse of salt water (lavage) or tiny tissue biopsies, to check for infection, inflammation or cancer. Read more about bronchoscopy .

sections.heading: Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) biopsy
sections.text: A special kind of bronchoscopy, also done while you are sedated. The scope has a small ultrasound probe on the end that uses sound waves to "see" through the airway wall. This lets the doctor find enlarged lymph nodes or lumps next to the airways and take a sample with a fine needle.

sections.heading: Thoracentesis
sections.text: A procedure to drain fluid that has built up around the lungs. After a numbing shot, a needle is placed between the ribs, usually guided by ultrasound for safety. Removing the fluid can make breathing easier, and testing it helps find the cause.

sections.heading: Restless Legs Syndrome
sections.text: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) causes an uncomfortable feeling in the legs and a strong urge to move them. It is usually worse in the evening and at night, especially when you are lying down or sitting still, and moving your legs brings relief. It can make it hard to fall asleep and stay asleep. Once it is diagnosed, treatment helps many people.

sections.heading: What is restless legs syndrome?
sections.text: RLS is a common condition of the nervous system. People describe the feeling in many ways: crawling, tingling, prickling, pulling or aching deep inside the legs. It is hard to describe, but it comes with a strong urge to move. Walking, stretching or rubbing the legs helps for a while. Most people notice the symptoms less during the day and more in the evening or at night, especially as they are trying to fall asleep. For many, the symptoms fade by early morning, which is when they finally get their most refreshing sleep.

sections.heading: Signs to look for
sections.text: An urge to move your legs, usually with uncomfortable feelings in them Symptoms that start or get worse when you rest, lie down or sit for a long time, such as in the car or at the movies Relief when you move, walk or stretch Symptoms that are worse in the evening or at night Trouble falling asleep, and feeling tired during the day Many people with RLS also have leg jerks or kicks while they sleep, which can wake them or their bed partner.

sections.heading: What causes it?
sections.text: Often there is no clear cause, and RLS can run in families. It is also linked to: Low iron levels in the body Pregnancy, especially the last few months Kidney disease Nerve damage in the legs (neuropathy), for example from diabetes Some medicines, such as certain allergy, anti-nausea and antidepressant medicines

sections.heading: How is it diagnosed?
sections.text: There is no single test for RLS. Your doctor diagnoses it from your description of the symptoms and an exam. Blood tests can check your iron levels and look for other causes. If your sleep is badly disturbed, a sleep study may be suggested to look for leg movements during sleep and other sleep problems.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.text: Treatment depends on how often symptoms happen and how much they affect your sleep. Treating the cause. If your iron is low, iron supplements may help. Changing a medicine that makes RLS worse can also help. Don't stop any medicine without talking to your doctor first. Medicines. Once diagnosed, many patients find that medicine relieves their symptoms. Your doctor will help choose the right one.

sections.heading: Things you can do at home
sections.text: Keep a regular sleep schedule. Get regular, moderate exercise, but not right before bed. Cut back on caffeine, alcohol and nicotine, especially in the evening. Try a warm bath, leg massage or gentle stretching before bed. Keep your mind busy when you have to sit still, for example with a book or puzzle. If restless legs are keeping you up at night, talk to us. Better sleep is possible.

sections.heading: Sarcoidosis
sections.text: Sarcoidosis causes tiny clumps of inflamed cells, called granulomas, to form in the body. It most often affects the lungs and the lymph nodes in the chest. No one knows exactly what causes it. It is not contagious. Many people have mild sarcoidosis that gets better on its own. Others need treatment and regular checkups.

sections.heading: What is sarcoidosis?
sections.text: Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory disease. The body's immune system forms tiny lumps called granulomas. Under a microscope they look like grains of sugar or sand. They can grow and clump together, and if too many form in one organ, that organ may not work as well. Sarcoidosis usually starts in the lungs or in the lymph nodes in the chest, but it can affect almost any part of the body, including the skin, eyes, joints and heart. In many people it goes away on its own within a few months to a few years; in others it lasts much longer.

sections.heading: What causes sarcoidosis?
sections.text: Doctors believe it starts when the immune system overreacts to something, such as bacteria, a virus, dust or chemicals, or mistakenly attacks the body's own healthy cells. The exact trigger is unknown. Possible causes being studied include: An infection with a virus or bacteria A problem in the immune system Something in the environment, such as a dust or chemical Genes passed down in families

sections.heading: Who gets sarcoidosis?
sections.text: It affects tens of thousands of people in the United States. It can happen at any age, but it is most common in young adults between 20 and 40. African Americans and people of Scandinavian, German or Irish descent are more likely to get it. African-American women get it about twice as often as African-American men.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
sections.text: Many people have no symptoms at all, and sarcoidosis is found by chance on a routine chest X-ray. When the lungs are involved, people may have: Shortness of breath A cough that won't go away

sections.heading: Other signs and symptoms
sections.text: Feeling tired or generally unwell Fever and night sweats Trouble sleeping Weight loss or loss of appetite Small red bumps on the face, arms or buttocks Red, tender bumps on the shins, often with aching ankles, wrists or other joints Red, watery or painful eyes, or blurry vision. See an eye doctor if you notice eye changes.

sections.heading: How is sarcoidosis diagnosed?
sections.text: No single test can prove you have sarcoidosis, and its symptoms look like those of other illnesses. So doctors also rule out conditions such as tuberculosis, lymphoma (cancer of the lymph nodes), rheumatoid arthritis and fungal infections. Tests may include: A chest X-ray, usually first, and sometimes a CT scan Breathing tests and blood tests A biopsy: a small sample of tissue, often taken from the lungs or lymph nodes during a bronchoscopy , to look at under a microscope

sections.heading: How serious is sarcoidosis?
sections.text: For many people it is mild, and the inflammation gets better on its own. For others it comes and goes, or stays the same without getting worse. In a small number of people it slowly gets worse over the years and leaves scar tissue in the lungs, skin, eyes or other organs, which can affect how they work. Rarely, when vital organs such as the heart are badly affected, sarcoidosis can be life-threatening.

sections.heading: How is sarcoidosis treated?
sections.text: Watching and waiting. If only the lungs and nearby lymph nodes are affected and you feel well, you may not need treatment. Sarcoidosis often clears on its own at this stage. Your doctor will check on you with regular visits and chest X-rays, often for 3 to 12 months. Medicines are usually recommended if the inflammation is getting worse or not improving, or if the heart, eyes or nervous system are involved, or the calcium level in your blood is high. The most common medicine is a steroid called prednisone, which calms the inflammation. Regular follow-up. If you take prednisone long-term, a doctor with experience in sarcoidosis should manage your care and watch for side effects. Not smoking, avoiding dust and fumes, and keeping up with checkups and eye exams all help protect your health.

sections.heading: Sleep Apnea
sections.text: Sleep apnea is a condition where your breathing stops or becomes very shallow many times during sleep. Loud snoring and feeling tired after a full night's sleep are common signs. Most people with sleep apnea don't know they have it. Left untreated, it raises the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke and diabetes. Treatment works well.

sections.heading: What is sleep apnea?
sections.text: "Apnea" means a pause in breathing. With sleep apnea, your breathing stops, or the airflow drops a lot, again and again while you sleep. This can happen many times every hour. Each time, your body wakes up briefly to start breathing again, usually without you noticing. There are two main types: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is the most common. When you fall asleep, the muscles in your throat relax. The soft tissue at the back of the throat can collapse and block the airway, and if you sleep on your back, your tongue can fall back too. A narrowed airway makes the tissue vibrate as you breathe, which causes snoring. A blocked airway stops the air completely. Central sleep apnea is less common and harder to diagnose. The airway stays open, but the brain doesn't send the signal to breathe. It is usually caused by nerve or muscle problems or other health conditions.

sections.heading: What are the signs?
sections.text: Loud, irregular snoring, sometimes with gasping or choking Waking up tired even after a full night in bed Feeling sleepy during the day, or falling asleep without meaning to, even while driving Low energy Morning headaches Trouble concentrating or a short attention span Getting up often at night to urinate Weight gain Anxiety or depression Often a bed partner is the first to notice the snoring or the pauses in breathing.

sections.heading: Who is at risk?
sections.text: Excess weight. This is the biggest risk. Your risk is higher if your body mass index (BMI) is 25 or more, and higher still at 30 or more. But slim people can have sleep apnea too. A large neck. 17 inches or more for men, or 16 inches or more for women. A thicker neck has more soft tissue that can block the airway. Age. It can happen at any age but is more common from young adulthood through middle age and beyond. Being male. Men get it more often than women, though women's risk goes up after menopause. High blood pressure , which is very common in people with sleep apnea. Family history. Traits that run in families, such as body shape or a small or set-back jaw, raise the risk. So can shared habits like diet and activity level.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Each pause in breathing lowers the oxygen in your blood and puts stress on your body. Over time, untreated sleep apnea can lead to high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, an irregular heartbeat, and pre-diabetes or diabetes. Daytime sleepiness also raises the risk of accidents at work and on the road.

sections.heading: How is it diagnosed?
sections.text: A sleep test measures your breathing, oxygen level and heart rate while you sleep. Depending on your situation, this may be a home sleep apnea test you do in your own bed, or an overnight sleep study in our sleep lab .

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.text: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) is the most common treatment. A small machine gently blows air through a mask while you sleep to keep your airway open. Most people sleep much better and feel more alert within days or weeks. An oral appliance , a mouthpiece made by a dentist that holds your jaw forward, can help some people with mild to moderate sleep apnea. Lifestyle changes : losing weight, sleeping on your side, and avoiding alcohol and sleeping pills before bed. Surgery or other devices may be options for some people who can't use CPAP. Central sleep apnea is treated by managing the cause and, in some cases, with special breathing machines. If you snore loudly or often feel tired during the day, talk to us about a sleep test.

sections.heading: (B) How is the sleep study performed?
sections.text:
When you are ready to go to bed, the Registered Polysomnographer (sleep technician) will
                            place
                            electrodes on your chin, scalp, outer edge of your eyelids, and legs. Monitors that record
                            your
                            heart rate and breathing will be attached to your chest. A video camera records your
                            movements
                            during sleep. The sleep technician will directly observe you while you sleep and note any
                            changes in your sleep, breathing, and heart rate. The number of times you stop breathing
                            will
                            be recorded. Signals from electrodes are recorded while you are awake (with your eyes
                            closed)
                            and during sleep. The time it takes you to fall asleep is measured, as well as the time it
                            takes you to enter REM (dreaming) sleep. The sensors, which are glued or taped to you, monitor
                            your
                            body while you sleep. These sensors are painless. Make sure to tell the technologist if you
                            are
                            allergic or sensitive to any adhesives. The sensors measure your: Brain waves Chin muscle activity Heart rate Breathing Oxygen levels Leg movements The wires are long enough to let you move around and turn over in bed. At the start of the
                            test, you will be asked to move your eyes, clench your teeth and move your legs. This will
                            make sure that the sensors are working. You are free to read until your normal bedtime. When it is time for you to try to go to
                            sleep, the lights will go off and a low-light video camera will allow the technologist to
                            see you from a nearby room. If a sensor comes loose or you need to go to the bathroom
                            during the night, the technologist will have to help you with the wires. Many patients do not sleep as well as they would at home. This may be because of the
                            sensors or the unfamiliar environment. This typically does not affect the results. Nearly
                            everyone falls asleep during an in-lab study. In most cases, you do not need a full eight
                            hours of sleep for the doctor to make a diagnosis. Occasionally, you may be prescribed
                            medication to help you sleep during the in-lab sleep study. In the morning, the technologist will test and then remove the sensors. The in-lab study is
                            complete once you are awake and the sensors have been removed.

sections.heading: (C) Why are sleep studies performed?
sections.text:
The test is done to diagnose possible sleep disorders, including: Excessive daytime sleepiness,
                                snoring Obstructive sleep apnea and other
                                breathing difficulties during sleep Insomnia Narcolepsy Periodic limb movement disorder
                                (frequent movements of the legs during sleep) REM behavior disorder (a condition
                                where you "act out" your dreams) Determine why a treatment for a
                                sleep disorder is not working
